title.en: The Little Unicorn and the Lost Rainbow

content:
In a valley made of clouds there lived a little unicorn named Luna. Her mane had seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. When the wind blew through it, she looked like a small piece of rainbow that had learned to walk. Every morning Luna climbed the hill, shook her mane gently at the sky, and all the flowers in the valley woke up.
But one morning the rain stopped and the sky stayed grey. Luna looked left. She looked right. The rainbow that always hung beyond the mountain was gone. She asked the little stream, "Have you seen the rainbow?" The stream only rattled its pebbles. She asked the bird on the branch, "You fly so high. Have you seen it?" The bird tilted its head and said, "Early today I saw seven bright pieces, and the wind carried them away."
So Luna went looking. She walked across the soft grass. The first piece, red, was lying in the strawberry patch, making the berries sweeter. The second, orange, rested on the edge of a roof like a tiny lamp. The third, yellow, sat on a dandelion puff and swayed whenever the breeze passed. Luna did not pick any of them up. She only whispered, "Later, may I borrow a little of your light?"
She walked on. Green was hiding in the lily pad under a sleepy frog. Blue was floating in the middle of a small pond. Indigo was tucked inside a morning glory that had folded itself shut. And the last piece, violet, had landed on a woollen scarf that an old woman had hung out to dry. All seven colours were found, but they were scattered so far apart that none of them could reach the others.
Luna stood in the middle of the valley and thought for a long time. Then she did something very slowly. One by one, she gave away the seven colours of her own mane to each small piece of light. The strawberry patch glowed. The roof glowed. The dandelion, the lily pad, the pond, the folded flower and the woollen scarf all began to glow too. From seven different places, the light stretched out its hands, and across the grey sky it joined again into one quiet, curving bridge.
The bridge was paler than before, but much wider. A bird flew under it and caught a little orange on one wing. The stream ran beneath it and carried a streak of blue. The old woman looked up and smiled. "Today's rainbow," she said, "seems to have grown right out of our own homes."
Luna was tired now, and the colour in her mane had almost faded away. She walked slowly home, and when she passed the pond she looked down. A very small rainbow was lying in the water, following her quietly.
The sky grew dark. Every place that had lent its light still held a little soft glow. The strawberries were asleep. The dandelion had closed its puff. The frog had pulled the lily pad up like a blanket. Luna lay down in her warm hay, shut her eyes, and felt her mane begin to grow warm again.
If you look out tonight and the sky seems a little grey, do not worry. The light has not been lost. It has only spread itself out, resting in the small things beside you, waiting for morning to become a bridge again. For now, close your eyes. Good night, little Luna. And good night to you.

title.en: The Rabbit Who Lived on the Moon

content:
A small white rabbit lives on the moon. Not in a palace and not in a cave, but in a round little hollow on the far side, a place so quiet that it can hear its own heart beating. Every evening, as soon as the sun goes down, the rabbit picks up a silver basket and begins one slow circle around the earth.
The basket holds sleepiness. It looks like very fine silver dust, so light that even the wind cannot move it. Only the rabbit knows how to scatter it. A pinch over the rooftops. A pinch over the treetops. And at every window where a lamp is still on, it leaves a slightly bigger pinch on the sill. The children who receive it give one small yawn, put down their toys, and slowly slip under the blanket.
The rabbit had done this work for a very long time and had never made a mistake. But one night, coming around to this side of the earth, it found a window that stayed bright. Inside, a child turned over, then turned over again, eyes wide open. The rabbit scattered a pinch of silver dust. Nothing. It scattered another. Still nothing. It took the softest cloud from its basket and laid it along the sill, but the child only looked at it and went back to counting the little shadows on the ceiling.
The rabbit grew worried. It sat down on the edge of the windowsill with both ears drooping, and wondered whether tonight's sleepiness was simply not strong enough. The basket was nearly empty. So it stopped scattering. It decided to stay and sit with this child for a while.
In a very small voice it began to describe the place where it lived. There is no wind on the moon, it said, and no sound of cars, only soft light lying on the ground like a warm blanket. There is a round hollow on the far side just big enough for one rabbit to curl up in, and once you lie down there even your shadow feels lighter. Going once around the earth is really very slow, it said, slow enough to watch every single window and see how the lamps go out one by one.
The child did not answer, only turned a face toward the sill. The rabbit kept talking, more slowly now, as slowly as a drop of water falling into a deep well. On the third time it said "there is no wind on the moon", the child's eyelids moved. On the fourth time, the breathing grew long and even.
The rabbit stood up very carefully and tipped the last of the moonlight out of its basket into the corner of the windowsill. The light was not bright. It only made the room feel a little less dark. Then it pushed the softest cloud a bit farther in, just enough to cover the thin cool line under the window.
It picked up the empty basket and went on. There were still many windows waiting. But tonight it walked more slowly than usual, because it would remember this one, and because it had learned something: sometimes sleepiness does not fall from a basket. Sometimes it arrives because someone is willing to sit down and quietly describe a peaceful place.
If you are still awake tonight, there is no hurry. The rabbit is coming around again with its basket. When it reaches your sill, it will sit for a moment before it begins the story of the little hollow on the far side of the moon. You can close your eyes now and just listen. Good night.

Long, long ago, in a valley full of ferns, there lived a little dinosaur named Bobo. Bobo had small round spots along his back, a very short tail, and one favourite thing to do: tilt his head and look up at the sky.
All the other dinosaurs in the valley had long necks. Each night they simply stretched up and could touch the lowest stars, and every star they touched gave a tiny ding and shone a little brighter. When it was Bobo's turn, he stood on tiptoe and stretched his neck as far as it would go, but the stars were still much, much too far away.
"I will reach them when I am bigger," Bobo told himself every single night. He practised stretching. He practised jumping. He practised standing on the tallest rock in the valley. Once he jumped so hard that he landed in a pile of soft ferns and got green leaves stuck all over his head. The big dinosaurs laughed kindly, but Bobo still felt a little sad.
At the edge of the valley lived a very old tortoise, with fine lines all over its shell like a map. That evening it watched Bobo standing on tiptoe again, and came slowly over. "Little one," it said, "stars are not something you reach." Bobo blinked. "Then how do you get them?" The tortoise drew its head a little way into its shell. "You wait for them. You do not have to stretch up at all. You only have to lie down, keep still, and let the sky grow dark by itself."
Bobo was not sure he believed that. But he was too tired to jump again. So he walked out into the grass, laid his belly against the warm earth that still held the day's sunshine, flattened his short tail, rested his chin on his two front paws, and did absolutely nothing.
At first, nothing happened. The wind walked through the ferns. A small beetle circled his ear twice. Somewhere far away someone gave a long yawn. Bobo very nearly got up again. And just then, the deepest blue above him turned a deeper blue still, and the first star lit up.
Nobody had touched it. It simply lit itself, small and light, as if someone had quietly struck a match after dark. Then came a second, and a third. Bobo hardly dared to breathe, in case one puff made them go out. But more and more stars arrived, until the whole sky was quietly full of them, hanging there, needing nobody to reach them at all.
Then Bobo understood what the old tortoise meant. All this time he had thought you had to grow tall enough to take a star. But if you simply lay down and looked up, the entire sky was yours. He smiled a small smile, and the grass blades swayed with it.
He fell asleep right there in the grass. A little dew came in the night, and the ferns sheltered him. In the morning he woke with one round leaf stuck to his back, like a green star someone had placed there while he slept.
After that, Bobo never stood on tiptoe again. Every evening he went back to the same patch of grass, lay down, rested his chin on his paws, and waited for the sky to darken. Sometimes the first star came early, sometimes a little later, but it always came.
You can try it tonight. No standing up, no stretching out a hand. Just let your back settle, let the blanket hold you softly, and wait a while. After your eyes close, the stars will still come out. Only this time they will be shining on the inside. Good night, little Bobo.

title.en: The Star That Forgot How to Shine

content:
High in the sky there was a very small star. Everyone called it Twinkle. It was the smallest of them all, hanging a little lower than the others, close to the top of a very tall pine tree. Small as it was, every night it shone carefully, just as brightly as anyone else.
But one evening, after the sky had gone dark, Twinkle could not shine at all. It tried the way it always did, pushing the light gently outward from its middle, and nothing happened. It tried again. Still dark. All around, the other stars came on one by one, and the moon stepped out from behind a cloud. Only the little place where Twinkle belonged stayed empty and black.
"Moon," Twinkle asked softly, "do you remember how to shine?" The moon was busy laying light across the sea and called back, "I have always just done it. I never had to think about it." Twinkle asked the wind, but the wind rushed past with only, "I am in a hurry. Ask me later." It asked the big star beside it, and the big star said, "Do not worry. Try a little harder."
Twinkle tried harder, until it trembled, and still there was no light. Suddenly it felt embarrassed, as if the whole sky were waiting for it to fill that one small gap, and it could not. So it moved slowly behind a thick cloud and hid. The cloud was soft and dark, which was exactly right.
It stayed hidden a long time. Below the cloud stood a small house with one window, and at the window sat a child, looking up and counting stars. "One, two, three..." At the spot where Twinkle usually hung, the child stopped. "Oh," it said, "the little star is not shining tonight."
From behind the cloud, Twinkle listened for the disappointed part. But the child thought for a moment, picked up a small night lamp from the table, turned it toward the sill, and switched it on. A bit of warm yellow light settled on the glass and reached a short way upward. "That's all right," the child said. "I will shine for you tonight."
Twinkle went very still. It looked at that small light coming up from the ground, so faint that it could not reach the cloud, let alone the sky, yet pointing faithfully toward the place where Twinkle was hiding. And it remembered something it had not thought about in a very long time: it had never shone so that someone could count it, or so that the sky would be complete. It shone simply because it wanted to.
So Twinkle stopped trying. It only let out one quiet breath, the way you do when you wake in the morning, and opened its eyes. The light came. Not the tight, bright light from before, but something pale and gentle, just enough to leak around the edge of the cloud, rest on the top of the pine tree, and touch the window glass. The child did not notice. It only yawned, left the little lamp on, and slowly lay down.
That night Twinkle did not become the brightest star, and it did not go back to its old place. It stayed at the edge of the cloud with its small soft light, keeping one little lamp company until very late. The other stars spread across the sky as usual. Nobody noticed that anything was missing, or that anything had been added.
After that, Twinkle sometimes forgot again. When it did, it no longer panicked or hid very far. It simply waited a while, for a window down below to light up first, or for the feeling to come back on its own. It had learned that shining a little less is all right, and being dark for a while is all right too.
If there is a small lamp left on in your room tonight, that is good. It does not need to reach very far. It only needs to reach the place where you lie down. You can close your eyes now. Good night, Twinkle. And good night to the little lamp.

title.en: The Bear Who Collected Goodnight Clouds

content:
In a wooden house at the edge of the forest lived a small bear. It owned a clear glass jar, and inside the jar was not honey and not candy. It was clouds. To be exact, it was the softest goodnight clouds from the hour just before sunset.
Every evening, when the sun was almost down, the bear carried its jar up the hill. The clouds then were warmed by the last light, pink around the edges, and felt like cotton that had been hanging in the sunshine. Standing on tiptoe, the bear would pick one small cloud, place it in the jar, and press in the wooden stopper. One cloud a day, never more. Slowly the jar filled, and holding it was even more comforting than holding a jar of honey.
On this particular evening the clouds were especially fine. The bear picked a full one, so fluffy it nearly made the jar round. It hugged the jar and started for home, and met several friends along the way.
First came the squirrel, standing on a branch with its tail wrapped around itself. "The wind may be stronger tonight," it said. "My nest has a little gap." The bear looked up, opened the jar, pinched off one corner of cloud and handed it over. The squirrel tucked it into the nest and sank halfway in at once. "Just right," it whispered.
Farther along, the mother bird was worrying by her nest because the eggs got cold at night. The bear gave her a thin slice of cloud to lay across them, like a small blanket that breathed. By the reeds, a hedgehog was curled in the dry leaves, its spines rustling against them. The bear wound the softest wisp around the hedgehog, and the leaves stopped prickling.
Then there was the field mouse, a hare who never quite slept soundly, and the flat stone by the stream that warmed all day and grew cold too quickly after dark. Each time the bear gave a little away. By the time it reached the door of the wooden house, only a thin layer remained in the jar, so light it looked almost empty.
Just then the rain began. Not a heavy rain, but a fine, quiet one, cool on the tip of the nose. The bear stood under the eaves hugging the empty jar, not quite ready to go inside. Tonight, it thought, there would be no cloud for me.
But out of the rain came the squirrel first, carrying that one small corner. Then the mother bird flew in with her thin slice held on one wing. The hedgehog rolled slowly up with a wisp still around it. The field mouse and the hare came too, and together they even pushed the stream stone as far as the doorstep. One by one they put their little pieces back into the bear's jar. And something strange happened: all those small scraps, gathered together, began to swell. They rose into one big soft cloud, drifted out of the jar's mouth, and settled steadily under the eaves, like a bed just large enough for one small bear.
The bear climbed on. The cloud dipped gently and held him. The rain kept falling, but not a drop reached him. The friends went home, and before leaving, each took back one tiny cloud, no more than was needed for a single night.
Now the jar was truly empty, and the bear was not sad at all. Lying on the soft cloud, listening to the rain on the roof, one drop and then another, slower than anything else, it understood: clouds are not things you save up. They are things that grow bigger after you give them away.
Deep in the night the lamp in the wooden house went out. One small corner of the big cloud was still floating under the eaves, unclaimed. "Let that piece stay there," the bear said, "in case someone passes by in the middle of the night and needs somewhere to lean."
If your blanket feels a little cool tonight, do not worry. That small corner left under the eaves is being carried by the evening wind, drifting slowly toward you. When it settles, you will feel a little softer, and then a little softer still. All right now, close your eyes. Good night, little bear. And good night to you.

Once upon a time, a little girl was loved by everyone, but most of all by her grandmother, who made her a red velvet cape with a hood. Because she wore it so often, people called her Little Red Riding Hood.
One day her mother said, "Take this basket of cakes and wine to grandmother, who is not well. Stay on the path and do not wander."
Red Riding Hood set off through the woods. A Wolf wanted to eat her, but dared not in the open. He asked where she was going, and she told him. The Wolf ran ahead to grandmother's cottage, knocked, and when the old woman opened the door, he swallowed her up and put on her clothes in bed.
When Red Riding Hood arrived, she noticed grandmother looked strange.
"Grandmother, what big eyes you have!"
"All the better to see you, my dear."
"What big teeth you have!"
"All the better to eat you!" And the Wolf sprang at her.
But a passing woodsman heard the noise and rushed in. He saved Red Riding Hood and her grandmother, and they all sat down to the cakes together.
So, little one, remember to stay on your own safe path, and gentle helpers are never far away. Close your eyes now, and dream of warm cakes and safe woods.

There was once a kind girl whose father married a woman with two daughters of her own. After he died, the stepmother made the girl do all the work, and they called her Cinderella.
One day the Prince invited every maiden to a grand ball, hoping to choose a bride. Cinderella's stepmother said she could not go. But as she sat crying, her fairy godmother appeared and, with a wave, turned a pumpkin into a coach, mice into horses, and a ragged dress into a gown of silver with glass slippers.
"But the magic ends at midnight," said the godmother.
At the ball, the Prince danced only with Cinderella. As the clock began to strike twelve, she ran, leaving one glass slipper behind.
The Prince searched the kingdom for the maiden whose foot fit the slipper. When he came to Cinderella's house, her stepsisters tried and failed. Cinderella slipped her foot in, and it fit perfectly.
The Prince married her, and they lived with kindness in their hearts. So, little one, goodness is its own quiet magic. Close your eyes, and let sweet dreams carry you to the ball.

Once there was a princess named Snow White, with skin as white as snow and a kind heart. Her stepmother, the Queen, was jealous and asked her mirror every day who was fairest. When the mirror said Snow White, the Queen sent a huntsman to take her into the forest.
The huntsman could not harm her and told her to run. Snow White found a tiny cottage belonging to seven dwarfs, who let her stay if she kept house.
The Queen learned she was alive and came disguised as an old woman, offering a poisoned apple. Snow White bit it and fell into a deep sleep. The dwarfs could not wake her and laid her in a glass coffin.
One day a Prince rode by, saw her, and kissed her forehead. The apple slipped from her lips, and she awoke. The Prince took her to his castle, and the jealous Queen's vanity was ended.
So, little one, a kind heart sleeps safely and wakes to love. Close your eyes now, and let the dwarfs watch over your dreams.

A Princess once dropped her golden ball into a deep well. She cried, and a Frog offered to fetch it if she would be his friend and let him eat from her plate and sleep on her pillow. She promised, and the Frog brought the ball back.
At first the Princess did not want to keep her word, but her father said a promise must be kept. So the Frog came to the palace. That night, when he asked to sleep on her pillow, she lifted him gently, and suddenly he became a Prince, who had been cursed by a wicked fairy.
They became friends, and soon the Prince's kingdom and the Princess's were joined in happiness.
So, little one, keeping a promise can wake the magic hidden in the world. Close your eyes, and dream of golden balls and gentle frogs.

In a time of hunger, a woodcutter's wife led his two children, Hansel and Gretel, into the forest and left them there. But Hansel had dropped white pebbles on the way, and they followed them home by moonlight.
The next time, she took them deeper, and Hansel could only drop crumbs, which the birds ate. Lost, the children found a cottage made of bread, cakes, and sugar. An old woman invited them in, but she was a witch who meant to eat them.
Gretel was clever. When the witch told her to look in the oven, Gretel pushed the witch in and shut the door. The children found treasure, and a friendly duck carried them across the river home, where their father was overjoyed.
So, little one, when you are lost, be brave and clever, and you will find your way home. Close your eyes now, and let the pebbles of the moonlight guide your dreams.

On a cold New Year's Eve, a little girl walked barefoot through the snow, holding matches to sell. No one bought any, and she was too afraid to go home.
She sat in a corner and lit one match. In its warm glow she saw a great iron stove, then a table of roast goose, then a beautiful Christmas tree. With the last match, she saw her grandmother, who had loved her, smiling and reaching out.
"Take me with you," whispered the girl. And her grandmother took her up, and they flew together into the light and warmth, where there was no cold and no hunger.
So, little one, even on the coldest night, love keeps you warm. Close your eyes now, and let grandmother's light carry you to a soft, safe sleep.

There was an Emperor who loved fine clothes. Two swindlers came and said they could weave a cloth so wonderful that only the wise could see it. In truth, they wove nothing at all.
The Emperor sent them gold, and they pretended to work. When he sent ministers to look, each was afraid to seem foolish, so each said the cloth was beautiful.
At last the Emperor paraded through the city in his new clothes, which were no clothes at all. The people, not wanting to seem unwise, cried how splendid he looked.
Then a small child called out, "But the Emperor has nothing on!"
And everyone whispered the truth.
So, little one, it is always brave and kind to tell the simple truth. Close your eyes now, and dream of honesty as bright as the sun.
